explanation.text: The Logic: A perpetuity has no maturity, yet its price still has finite interest-rate sensitivity. The standard closed-form result is that the Macaulay duration of a level perpetuity equals (1 + y)/y, which for typical yields is closely approximated by 1/y. For example, at y = 10%, duration is approximately 10 years. The Trap: "Maturity / 2" and "10 years" are arbitrary numbers with no theoretical basis for a perpetuity. "Infinite" confuses maturity with duration — even an instrument with infinite maturity has a finite duration because distant cash flows are heavily discounted. Note: The Portfolio Managers (NISM-Series-XXI-B) workbook mentions perpetual bonds having no maturity and discusses duration/modified duration, but does not present an explicit duration formula for a perpetuity. The 1/y (and (1+y)/y) approximation is a general fixed-income result used here as industry-standard framing.
